[1] I dismiss this appeal for the reasons that follow.

[2] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his spouse, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, and their children XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellants) are citizens of Colombia. The Appellants allege that, if they return to Colombia, they will face persecution or serious harm at the hands of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia-People's Army (FARC-EP) because they refused to pay an extortion fee. XXXX XXXXandXXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX began working with their family's XXXX XXXX in 2015. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXand XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX owned and operated a XXXX XXXX in Bogotá for 10 years. In XXXX 2019, an individual claiming to be a member of the FARC-EP demanded that the Appellants pay an extortion fee. After asking around his area, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX found out that many businesses in his area had faced extortion demands. The Appellants paid extortion fees in XXXX and XXXX, but refused to pay in XXXX 2019, when advised of an increase in fees. The Appellants left Bogotá for their country home in XXXX where they received another threatening phone call. They left Colombia for the United States on in XXXX 2019 and crossed the border into Canada that same month. After their departure, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX father received a threatening message and visit from two individuals at his country home in XXXX asking about the Appellants and saying they never forget about debtors.

[3] The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) accepted the Appellants' allegations as credible except as indicated in its internal flight alternative analysis. The RPD found that the issue of an internal flight alternative was determinative. It found that the Appellants have a viable internal flight alternative in Barranquilla. As part of its internal flight alternative analysis, the RPD found that the Appellants had not demonstrated, on a balance of probabilities (in other words, that it was more likely than not), that the person extorting them was a member of the FARC. It also found that the Appellants had not established, on a balance of probabilities, that their agent of harm would have the means, interest and motivation to track them down in Barranquilla. It also found that it would not be unreasonable, in the circumstances of this case, to expect the Appellants to relocate to Barranquilla.
DECISION

[4] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 I do not agree with any of the arguments made by the Appellants' representative as to why she believes the RPD erred in this case. I find that the RPD was correct to find that the Appellants have a viable internal flight alternative in Barranquilla.

subthemes.text:
ANALYSIS

[5] I do not agree with the Appellants' representative that the RPD set a higher standard of proof than that required by requiring them to establish the identity of their agent of harm. I agree with the case law cited by the Appellants which has found that it is an error for the RPD to apply an incorrect legal test. However, the RPD did not apply an incorrect test in this case. While I agree with the Appellants that they may not be required to specifically identify the precise affiliation of their agents of harm, their inability to do so has implications for their ability to meet their onus under the internal flight alternative analysis. In this case, the RPD did not set a higher standard of proof by requiring the Appellants to identify the affiliation of their agent of harm. Instead, it correctly found that their inability to do so adversely affected their ability to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that their agent of harm had the means, interest and motivation to track them down in Barranquilla.
No error in finding a failure to establish that agent of harm was a member of FARC-EP

[6] The Appellants' representative argues that the RPD erred in finding that it was speculative for the Appellants to allege that the person extorting them was a member of the FARC because of his reference to needing funds for an important mobilization. She argues that it was no coincidence that the agent of harm disclosed "valuable information" by referring to the important mobilization given that a group of FARC members withdrew from the peace accord with the government shortly thereafter, in XXXX 2019. I do not find that the RPD erred in finding speculative the Appellants allegation that the agent of harm was a member of the FARC for this reason. It is speculative to suggest that the agent of harm's reference to a mobilization when requesting a higher extortion fee from the Appellants is connected to the withdrawal of certain FARC members from the peace process.

[7] I also find that the RPD correctly preferred to give more weight to the objective evidence in the National Documentation Package for Colombia which indicates that Bogotá is not a primary area of activity for FARC dissidents2 and evidence that local criminals often pose as members of the FARC when extorting merchants. The Appellants' representative argues that the fact that the NDP does not mention Bogotá as an area in which the FARC dissidents operate should not be understood as a lack of presence since FARC members have reinserted into society and this makes them more dangerous. I disagree. The research report referred to by the RPD specifically addresses the geographic location of activities by FARC dissidents. The report and map attached to it show that Bogotá is not an area of activity for these dissidents. Therefore, the RPD did not misconstrue this evidence.
RPD did not err in assessment of article

subthemes.text:
[8] The Appellants' representative argues that the RPD erred in refusing to give weight to an article that the Appellants' counsel before the RPD had submitted regarding the niece of Gabriel Garcia Marquez. The article in question states that Mr. Garcia Marquez's niece was kidnapped for four months in Santa Marta for 4 months in 2018 and released. Following her release, she received a death threat and fled the country. According to the Appellants' representative, the article demonstrates that the FARC operates in Santa Marta, which is a region that is geographically close to Barranquilla. I disagree with this argument.

[9] To begin, for the reasons set out above, the Appellants did not establish that the agent of harm in their case was a member of the FARC. In any event, the article does not identify who the kidnappers of Mr. Garcia Marquez's niece were. It simply states that "it could be established that the kidnapping ... was planned by Rigoberto Rojas Mendoza aka "the Scorpion," who was detained in Barranquilla." There is no mention of the FARC in the article.3 In my view, the RPD did not err in distinguishing the Appellants' circumstances from those of Mr. Garcia Marquez's niece and therefore according no weight to the article.
